decks.title: Agriculture in India — Part 1: Importance, problems and the Green Revolution
goals: Explain the importance of agriculture to India’s economy
Identify problems such as small holdings, dependence on the monsoon and soil degradation, and suggest remedies
Explain the meaning and inputs of the Green Revolution and evaluate its positive and negative impacts

slides.heading: Fields that feed a nation
slides.body_md: Part 1 — From the wheat fields of Punjab to the paddy of the Godavari delta and the tea gardens of Assam, farming shapes India’s landscape and economy. We look at why it matters, what holds it back, and how the **Green Revolution** changed it.

rows: Wheat and rice with tube wells
Cotton and millets on black and red soil

visual.alt: Table of four Indian regions and a typical farm scene in each

slides.narration: Namaste! Travel across India and you will see wheat in Punjab, paddy in the river deltas, tea on the hills of Assam and cotton on the black soils of the Deccan. Farming feeds the country and employs a huge number of people. In this part we ask why agriculture matters, what problems farmers face, and how the Green Revolution transformed Indian farming.

slides.heading: Why agriculture matters
slides.body_md: **Livelihood:** a very large part of India’s workers — nearly half (as of the early 2020s) — depend on farming. **Food security:** it feeds a population of over 1.4 billion (as of the early 2020s). **Raw materials:** cotton for the mills of Ahmedabad and Mumbai, jute for Kolkata, sugarcane for sugar mills, oilseeds for oil mills. **Exports:** rice, tea, spices, cotton, fruit. **Rural demand:** farm incomes buy fertilisers, tractors and consumer goods, helping industry. Its share of national income has fallen as industry and services grew, but it remains the base of the rural economy.

rows: Rice, wheat, pulses for the nation

visual.alt: Table of four roles of agriculture in India with examples

slides.narration: Agriculture matters for many reasons. Nearly half of India’s workers earn their living from it. It grows the food for well over a billion people. It feeds raw materials to the cotton, jute and sugar mills. Rice, tea and spices earn money abroad. And when farmers earn more, they buy tractors, fertilisers and goods, which helps industry too.

slides.heading: Problems and remedies
slides.body_md: **Small and fragmented holdings:** land divided among heirs into tiny scattered plots — remedy: **consolidation of holdings**, cooperative farming. **Dependence on the monsoon:** rain is uncertain and uneven; droughts and floods — remedy: irrigation, watershed management, drought-resistant crops. **Soil degradation:** erosion, loss of fertility, waterlogging and salinity — remedy: contour ploughing, crop rotation, balanced fertiliser, drainage. **Low yields and outdated methods**, **lack of cheap credit** (debt to moneylenders), **poor storage and marketing** — remedies: better seeds, **Kisan Credit Card** and cooperative banks, crop insurance, cold storage, regulated markets and minimum support prices.

visual.alt: Table of five problems of Indian agriculture and a remedy for each

slides.narration: Indian farmers face several problems. Land is divided among heirs until each owns a few tiny, scattered plots. Many fields depend on uncertain monsoon rain. Soils lose fertility, and some become waterlogged or salty. Farmers often lack cheap loans, good storage and fair markets. Remedies include joining plots together, more irrigation, careful soil care, bank credit, crop insurance and support prices.

slides.heading: Fragmented holdings and consolidation
slides.body_md: An illustrative farm near Muzaffarpur in Bihar has **5 scattered plots** (0.5, 1.2, 0.3, 0.9, 1.1 ha). The farmer wastes time walking between them, cannot install one well or use a tractor easily, and boundary ridges waste land. **Consolidation of holdings** (chakbandi) exchanges plots so each farmer gets one compact block of about the same total area — here **4 ha**.

slides.narration: Here is an imaginary farm in Bihar split into five small plots scattered around the village. The farmer walks from plot to plot, cannot run one well or tractor across all of them, and loses land to boundary ridges. Consolidation swaps plots between farmers so that each one gets a single compact block of the same total area, which is far easier to farm.

slides.heading: Worked example: diagnosing a farm’s problems
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A groundnut farmer near Anantapur in Andhra Pradesh has three small plots, no well, and borrows from a moneylender each season. Last year the July rains failed. Identify three problems and suggest a remedy for each.

**Step 1. Monsoon dependence:** no irrigation, so a delayed monsoon ruins the crop → farm ponds, drip irrigation, drought-tolerant varieties.

**Step 2. Fragmented holding:** three plots waste time and effort → consolidation.

**Step 3. Costly credit:** moneylender’s high interest → Kisan Credit Card or cooperative bank loan, plus crop insurance.

visual.alt: Flow from rain failure to crop loss and debt, ending in remedies

slides.narration: This farmer near Anantapur depends wholly on the monsoon, so when the July rains fail his groundnut crop is lost. His land is split into three plots, which wastes effort. And he borrows from a moneylender at high interest. The remedies follow from the problems: farm ponds or drip irrigation, consolidation of his plots, and a bank loan through a Kisan Credit Card with crop insurance.

slides.heading: The Green Revolution: meaning and inputs
slides.body_md: In the mid-1960s, after droughts and food shortages, India adopted a package of new methods that sharply raised the output of food grains, especially **wheat** (later **rice**). This is called the **Green Revolution**. Inputs: **high-yielding variety (HYV) seeds** (dwarf wheat from Mexico, developed further in India under scientists such as M. S. Swaminathan); **assured irrigation** (canals, tube wells); **chemical fertilisers** and **pesticides**; **farm machinery**; **credit** and **minimum support prices**. It spread first in **Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh**.

nodes.label: Much higher yields of wheat and rice

visual.alt: Flow of the inputs of the Green Revolution leading to higher yields

slides.narration: In the middle of the nineteen sixties India faced droughts and had to import food. It then adopted a package of new methods: high yielding seeds of wheat and later rice, assured irrigation from canals and tube wells, chemical fertilisers and pesticides, machines, cheap credit and support prices. Yields jumped, first in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh. This change is called the Green Revolution.

slides.narration: This chart shows imaginary wheat yields in one district. Before the new seeds, a hectare gave about one tonne. Within twenty years it gave nearly three, and by the end of the century over four. Remember that yield means production divided by the area under the crop. The biggest gains came where water and fertiliser were assured, as in the irrigated plains of the north-west.

slides.heading: Worked example: reading the yield chart
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Using District P’s data, (a) find the percentage rise in yield from 1960 to 1980, and (b) explain the rise.

**(a)** Rise $= \dfrac{2.8 - 1.0}{1.0} \times 100 = 180$%.

**(b)** HYV wheat seeds were sown widely; canals and tube wells gave assured water; fertiliser use rose; farmers received credit and support prices, so they could invest in inputs.

visual.alt: Table of illustrative wheat yields of District P from 1960 to 2000

slides.narration: To find the percentage rise, subtract the old yield from the new, divide by the old yield and multiply by one hundred. Here the yield almost trebled, a rise of one hundred and eighty per cent. The reasons are the new seeds, assured water from canals and tube wells, more fertiliser, and credit and fixed prices that let farmers buy these inputs.

slides.heading: Impact of the first Green Revolution
slides.body_md: **Positive:** India became **self-sufficient in food grains** and stopped depending on food aid; **buffer stocks** guard against famine; farm incomes and rural jobs in agro-industries rose; demand for fertilisers, pumps and tractors helped industry. **Negative:** **regional inequality** — irrigated north-west gained, rain-fed regions lagged; **crop inequality** — wheat and rice gained, pulses and millets were neglected; **soil and water damage** — overuse of fertilisers, waterlogging and salinity, falling water tables in Punjab and Haryana; pesticide pollution; richer farmers gained more than small farmers.

visual.alt: Table of positive and negative impacts of the first Green Revolution

slides.narration: The Green Revolution made India self sufficient in food grains, built up buffer stocks against famine and raised farm incomes. But it had costs. Irrigated regions gained far more than dry ones. Wheat and rice gained while pulses and millets were neglected. Heavy use of water and chemicals has lowered water tables, made some soils salty and polluted streams, and richer farmers gained more than poor ones.

slides.narration: Quick check. Gains were concentrated in irrigated regions, widening the gap with dry regions.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Agriculture gives jobs to nearly half of workers (as of the early 2020s), food for all, raw materials and exports.
Problems: small, fragmented holdings; monsoon dependence; soil degradation; low yields; costly credit; poor storage and markets.
Remedies: consolidation, irrigation, soil conservation, credit, insurance, regulated markets, support prices.
Green Revolution: HYV seeds + irrigation + fertilisers; wheat and rice; Punjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh.
Impact: self-sufficiency and buffer stocks, but regional and crop inequality and soil-water damage.

visual.alt: Summary table of key words for each topic in Part 1

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Farming gives jobs to nearly half of India’s workers, food to everyone and raw materials to industry. Its problems include tiny holdings, uncertain rain, tired soils and costly credit, and each has a remedy. The Green Revolution used new seeds, water and fertiliser to make India self sufficient in grain, but it also widened inequalities and harmed soil and water.

decks.title: Agriculture in India — Part 2: Types of farming and agricultural seasons
goals: Distinguish subsistence from commercial farming and intensive from extensive farming
Describe the features of plantation and mixed farming with Indian examples
State the sowing and harvesting months of kharif, rabi and zayad and name two crops of each

slides.heading: Many ways to farm
slides.body_md: Part 2 — Indian farms range from tiny hill plots that feed one family to vast tea estates with their own factories. The type of farming depends on land, labour, capital, climate and markets. Crops also follow a calendar of **three seasons**.

rows: Hill farms of Mizoram and Uttarakhand
Grapes of Nashik; sugarcane of Maharashtra
Paddy of the Ganga delta and Kerala
Tea in Assam; rubber in Kerala

visual.alt: Table of five types of farming with an Indian example of each

slides.narration: Indian farms come in many types. A hill family may grow food only for itself, while a grape grower sells everything to traders. Some farmers squeeze two or three crops a year out of tiny plots, and tea estates cover whole hillsides with their own factories. In this part we compare these types and then learn the calendar of the three crop seasons.

slides.heading: Subsistence and commercial farming
slides.body_md: **Subsistence farming:** crops grown mainly to feed the farmer’s family; small plots, simple tools, family labour, little use of fertiliser; little surplus to sell; a mix of food crops. Examples: hill farms of the north-east and Uttarakhand, much of rain-fed central India. **Commercial farming:** crops grown mainly **for sale**; larger farms, purchased inputs (HYV seeds, fertilisers, machines), often one main crop. Examples: grapes of **Nashik**, sugarcane of western Maharashtra, wheat and rice of Punjab.

visual.alt: Table comparing subsistence and commercial farming

slides.narration: In subsistence farming the family grows food mainly for itself, on small plots with simple tools and family labour, and has little left to sell. In commercial farming crops are grown to be sold. Farms are larger and use bought seeds, fertilisers and machines, often for one main crop. The grape farms of Nashik and the sugarcane farms of Maharashtra are commercial.

slides.heading: Intensive and extensive farming
slides.body_md: **Intensive farming:** small holdings in densely populated areas; much **labour and inputs per hectare**; two or three crops a year (**multiple cropping**); **high yield per hectare**. Examples: the Ganga–Brahmaputra delta of West Bengal, coastal Kerala, Tamil Nadu deltas. **Extensive farming:** large farms in thinly populated areas; heavy use of **machines**, little labour per hectare; usually one crop a year; **low yield per hectare but high output per worker**. It is uncommon in India; large mechanised farms are found in only a few areas.

visual.alt: Table comparing intensive and extensive farming

slides.narration: Intensive farming is found where land is scarce and people are many, as in the delta of West Bengal or coastal Kerala. Farmers put a great deal of labour and manure into each small field and raise two or three crops a year, so the yield per hectare is high. Extensive farming uses large farms and machines with few workers. Each hectare yields less, but each worker produces much more.

slides.body_md: Classify a farm from its description.
slides.narration: Quick check. A family that grows food mainly for itself practises subsistence farming.

slides.heading: Plantation farming
slides.body_md: **Plantation farming** grows a **single cash crop** on a **large estate**. Features: large capital investment; many hired workers (often migrants), living on the estate; scientific methods; **processing on or near the estate** (tea factories); good transport links to ports and markets; output mostly for sale or export. Indian examples: **tea** in Assam (Brahmaputra valley), Darjeeling and the Nilgiris; **coffee** in Karnataka; **rubber** in Kerala; spices and coconut in the south. Many plantations were set up in the colonial period.

visual.alt: Flow from a plantation estate through processing and transport to sale

slides.narration: Plantation farming grows one cash crop on a very large estate. It needs plenty of money and many hired workers, who often live on the estate. The crop is usually processed nearby, as in the tea factories of Assam, and then sent by road or rail to ports and markets. Tea in Assam and Darjeeling, coffee in Karnataka and rubber in Kerala are grown this way.

slides.heading: Mixed farming
slides.body_md: **Mixed farming** combines **growing crops** with **rearing animals** (cattle, buffaloes, poultry) on the same farm. Crops provide fodder for animals; animal dung returns to the fields as manure; milk, eggs and meat give a **steady daily income** that cushions crop losses. Common in **Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh**, where wheat, rice and fodder crops are grown alongside dairy buffaloes, and in many villages across India.

visual.alt: Table of how crops, animals and the farm family support one another in mixed farming

slides.narration: Mixed farming means growing crops and keeping animals on the same farm. The fields supply fodder to cattle and buffaloes, and their dung goes back to the fields as manure. Milk gives the family money every day, even when a crop fails. Farms in Haryana and Punjab often grow wheat and fodder and keep dairy buffaloes in exactly this way.

slides.heading: Worked example: classifying farms
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Classify each farm and give a reason: (a) a 400-hectare tea estate near Dibrugarh with its own factory; (b) a half-hectare plot near Kozhikode giving two paddy crops and a vegetable crop each year; (c) a farm near Karnal growing wheat and fodder and selling buffalo milk; (d) a hill plot in Mizoram growing rice and maize for the family.

**(a)** Plantation — one crop, large estate, processing on site. **(b)** Intensive — tiny plot, three crops a year. **(c)** Mixed — crops plus dairy. **(d)** Subsistence — food for the family.

visual.alt: Table classifying four farms by type with the clue for each

slides.narration: Look for the clue in each description. A huge tea estate with its own factory is plantation farming. A tiny plot in Kerala that gives three crops a year is intensive farming. A Haryana farm with wheat, fodder and milk buffaloes is mixed farming. And a hill family growing rice and maize to eat is practising subsistence farming.

slides.heading: The three agricultural seasons
slides.body_md: **Kharif:** sown with the onset of the south-west monsoon (**June–July**), harvested **September–October** — rice, jowar, bajra, maize, cotton, groundnut, jute, soya bean. **Rabi:** sown **October–December** after the monsoon, harvested **March–April** — wheat, gram, mustard, barley, peas; helped by winter rain from western disturbances in the north-west. **Zayad:** a short season between rabi and kharif (**March–June**) on irrigated land — watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, vegetables, fodder.

slides.narration: India has three crop seasons. Kharif crops such as rice, cotton and maize are sown when the monsoon arrives in June and July and harvested in September and October. Rabi crops such as wheat, gram and mustard are sown from October to December and harvested in March and April. In between, from March to June, irrigated fields can grow quick zayad crops such as watermelon and cucumber.

slides.heading: Why the seasons differ
slides.body_md: **Kharif** crops need **heat and plenty of water**, which the monsoon provides. **Rabi** crops need a **cool growing period** and a **dry, sunny ripening period**; they use moisture stored in the soil, irrigation and light winter rain from **western disturbances** (Punjab, Haryana). **Zayad** crops are quick-growing and need **irrigation** because summer is hot and dry. With irrigation, one field can carry a kharif and a rabi crop — and sometimes a zayad crop — in a single year.

visual.alt: Table of the weather and water source for each season

slides.narration: The seasons suit different crops. Kharif crops love heat and water, which the monsoon supplies. Rabi crops need cool weather to grow and dry sunny days to ripen, and they draw on soil moisture, irrigation and gentle winter showers in the north-west. Zayad crops grow quickly in the hot dry months, so they need irrigation. With water, one field can carry two or even three crops a year.

slides.heading: Quick check: crop seasons
slides.body_md: Work out the season from sowing and harvesting months.
slides.narration: Quick check. Wheat sown in November is harvested in March or April.

slides.heading: Worked example: how hard is a field worked?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** An illustrative farm near Muzaffarpur has a **net sown area** of 4 ha. It grows rice on 4 ha in kharif, wheat on 3 ha in rabi and vegetables on 1 ha in zayad. Find (a) the gross cropped area and (b) the cropping intensity.

**(a)** Gross cropped area $= 4 + 3 + 1 = 8$ ha.

**(b)** Cropping intensity $= \dfrac{8}{4} \times 100 = 200$%. A value of 200% means each hectare carries two crops a year on average — intensive farming made possible by irrigation.

visual.alt: Table of crops and areas by season on an illustrative farm

slides.narration: Gross cropped area counts a field once for every crop it carries in the year, so we add the three seasons. Cropping intensity compares this with the net sown area: divide the gross area by the net area and multiply by one hundred. This farm scores two hundred, which means each hectare grows two crops a year on average, a sign of intensive farming with irrigation.

slides.narration: To sum up Part 2. Subsistence farmers grow food for themselves, while commercial farmers grow for the market. Intensive farming gets high yields from small plots with much labour, while extensive farming uses big machines on large farms. Plantations grow one cash crop on a large estate, and mixed farms combine crops with animals. Kharif, rabi and zayad crops follow the rhythm of the monsoon and the winter.

notes.title: Agriculture in India — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Importance of agriculture
sections.body_md:
- **Employment:** nearly half of India’s workers depend on farming (as of the early 2020s).
- **Food security:** food grains, pulses, oilseeds, fruit and vegetables for the whole population; buffer stocks.
- **Raw materials:** cotton (textile mills), jute (Kolkata jute mills), sugarcane (sugar mills), oilseeds (oil mills).
- **Exports:** rice, tea, spices, cotton, fruit.
- **Market for industry:** farmers buy fertilisers, pumps, tractors and consumer goods.
- Its share of national income has fallen as industry and services grew, but it remains the base of the rural economy.

key_terms.definition_md: An industry that uses farm produce as its raw material, such as cotton textiles, jute or sugar.

visual.alt: Table of farm products and the industries they supply

sections.heading: 2. Problems and remedies
sections.body_md:
| Problem | Effect | Remedy |
|---|---|---|
| Small, fragmented holdings | Wasted time; machines and wells hard to use | Consolidation (chakbandi); cooperative farming |
| Dependence on the monsoon | Droughts and floods ruin crops | Irrigation; watershed management; drought-resistant crops |
| Soil degradation | Erosion, lost fertility, waterlogging, salinity | Crop rotation; contour ploughing; balanced fertiliser; drainage |
| Low yields, old methods | Low incomes | Better seeds; training; extension services |
| Lack of cheap credit | Debt to moneylenders | Kisan Credit Card; cooperative and rural banks; crop insurance |
| Poor storage and marketing | Losses; low prices from middlemen | Cold storage; regulated markets; minimum support price |

key_terms.definition_md: The splitting of a farmer’s land into many small, scattered plots, usually through inheritance.
Regrouping a farmer’s scattered plots into one compact block of about the same total area.

visual.alt: Table of three problems and remedies

sections.heading: 3. The Green Revolution
sections.body_md:
- **Meaning:** a sharp rise in the output of food grains (mainly wheat, later rice) from the mid-1960s through a package of modern inputs.
- **Inputs:** HYV seeds; assured irrigation (canals, tube wells); chemical fertilisers; pesticides; farm machines; credit; minimum support prices.
- **Where:** first in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh (irrigated plains).
- **Positive:** self-sufficiency in food grains; buffer stocks; higher farm incomes; growth of agro-industries and rural jobs.
- **Negative:** regional inequality (rain-fed areas left behind); crop inequality (pulses, millets neglected); overuse of groundwater and falling water tables; waterlogging and salinity; pesticide pollution; small farmers gained less.

key_terms.definition_md: The large increase in food-grain production in India from the mid-1960s using HYV seeds, irrigation and fertilisers.
High-yielding variety seeds that give much larger harvests when given enough water and fertiliser.

visual.alt: Table of two positive and two negative effects of the Green Revolution

sections.heading: 4. Types of farming
sections.body_md:
| Type | Key features | Indian example |
|---|---|---|
| Subsistence | Food for family; small plots; family labour | Hill farms of Mizoram, Uttarakhand |
| Commercial | Crops for sale; bought inputs; often one crop | Grapes of Nashik; sugarcane of Maharashtra |
| Intensive | Small farms; much labour per hectare; multiple cropping; high yield per hectare | Ganga delta of West Bengal; coastal Kerala |
| Extensive | Large farms; machines; one crop; low yield per hectare, high output per worker | Uncommon in India |
| Plantation | One cash crop; large estate; capital; hired labour; processing on site | Tea (Assam), coffee (Karnataka), rubber (Kerala) |
| Mixed | Crops plus livestock; dung as manure; fodder from crops | Punjab, Haryana |

key_terms.definition_md: Large-scale growing of a single cash crop on an estate using much capital, hired labour and on-site processing.
Growing crops and rearing animals together on the same farm.

visual.alt: Table of three farming types with examples

sections.heading: 5. Agricultural seasons
sections.body_md:
| Season | Sown | Harvested | Crops |
|---|---|---|---|
| Kharif | June–July (monsoon onset) | September–October | Rice, jowar, bajra, maize, cotton, groundnut, jute, soya bean |
| Rabi | October–December | March–April | Wheat, gram, mustard, barley, peas |
| Zayad | March | June | Watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, vegetables, fodder |

Rabi crops benefit from winter rain brought by western disturbances in the north-west. Zayad crops need irrigation.

key_terms.definition_md: The crop season that begins with the south-west monsoon; crops are sown in June–July and harvested in September–October.
The winter crop season; crops are sown in October–December and harvested in March–April.
A short summer season between rabi and kharif for quick, irrigated crops such as melons and cucumbers.

visual.alt: Table of the three seasons and their months

sections.heading: 6. Working with farm data
sections.body_md:
- **Yield** = production ÷ area (for example tonnes per hectare).
- **Percentage change** = (new − old) ÷ old × 100.
- **Gross cropped area** = total of the areas sown in all seasons of the year.
- **Cropping intensity** = gross cropped area ÷ net sown area × 100; above 100 means fields carry more than one crop a year.

key_terms.definition_md: Gross cropped area as a percentage of net sown area; it shows how many crops a field carries in a year.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing that the Green Revolution helped all crops and all regions equally.
- Confusing kharif and rabi months.
- Calling mixed farming a mix of crops only (it must include animals).
- Dividing area by production for yield.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Problems (1 mark each): problem with its effect; remedy that matches.
- Green Revolution (3 marks): inputs, region, crops; or three effects.
- Seasons (2–3 marks): sowing and harvesting months with two crops.
- Data (2–3 marks): working shown, answer with unit.

questions.stem_md: State three positive effects of the first Green Revolution on India.

answer.model_answer_md: India became self-sufficient in food grains and no longer depended on imported food aid; large buffer stocks were built up to guard against drought and famine; farm incomes rose in the irrigated north-west, creating rural jobs and demand for fertilisers, pumps and tractors made by Indian industry.

questions.solution_md: Self-sufficiency; buffer stocks; incomes and industry.

questions.stem_md: Evaluate the impact of the first Green Revolution on (a) India’s food supply, (b) the soil and water of Punjab and (c) small farmers.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Strongly positive: wheat and rice output rose sharply, India became self-sufficient in food grains and built buffer stocks. (b) Negative: heavy irrigation and fertiliser use caused falling water tables, waterlogging, salinity and chemical pollution. (c) Mixed: richer farmers with land, wells and credit gained most, while many small and rain-fed farmers could not afford the inputs and gained little.

questions.solution_md: Food positive; soil-water negative; small farmers mixed.

questions.stem_md: Suggest two ways in which farmers in Punjab could reduce the damage the Green Revolution has done to their soil and water.

answer.model_answer_md: Use drip or sprinkler irrigation and grow less water-hungry crops such as maize or pulses in place of some rice, so less groundwater is pumped; apply fertiliser according to soil tests, add organic manure and rotate crops with legumes to restore soil health.

questions.solution_md: Save water; restore soil.

options.text_md: commercial farming

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between intensive and extensive farming with reference to (a) size of farms and use of labour and (b) yield.

questions.stem_md: Describe three characteristics of the tea estates of Assam that make them plantation farms.

answer.model_answer_md: Each estate grows a single cash crop, tea, over hundreds of hectares; it needs large capital and employs many hired workers who often live on the estate; the leaves are processed in the estate’s own factory and the tea is sent by road, rail or river to Kolkata or Guwahati for sale and export.

questions.solution_md: Single crop on large estate; capital and labour; processing and market.

questions.stem_md: Give two advantages of mixed farming for a farmer in Haryana.

questions.solution_md: Steady income; dung and fodder recycling.

questions.stem_md: Compare a hill farm in Uttarakhand that grows food for the family with a sugarcane farm in western Maharashtra that supplies a sugar mill, under the headings (a) purpose, (b) size and (c) inputs.

(b) The hill farm is a few small terraced plots; the sugarcane farm is larger and compact. (c) The hill farm uses family labour, simple tools and manure; the sugarcane farm uses irrigation, fertilisers, improved varieties and hired labour or machines.

questions.solution_md: Purpose; size; inputs.

answer.model_answer_md: Rabi: wheat and gram (also mustard, barley, peas). Zayad: watermelon and cucumber (also muskmelon, vegetables, fodder).

questions.stem_md: State the sowing and harvesting months of the kharif, rabi and zayad seasons.

answer.model_answer_md: Kharif: sown in June–July with the onset of the monsoon, harvested in September–October. Rabi: sown in October–December, harvested in March–April. Zayad: sown around March, after the rabi harvest, and harvested by June.

questions.solution_md: Months for each season.

questions.stem_md: A farmer near Meerut in western Uttar Pradesh grows rice in kharif and wheat in rabi on the same field. Explain how the seasons and irrigation make this possible.

answer.model_answer_md: Rice grows in the hot, wet monsoon months from June to October and is harvested in time for wheat to be sown in November, which grows through the cool winter and is harvested in April. questions.solution_md: Two seasons in sequence; irrigation.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Give two reasons why agriculture is important to India. [2]

(b) What is meant by fragmentation of holdings? State one harmful effect. [2]

(c) Explain why dependence on the monsoon is a problem for Indian farmers and suggest two remedies. [3]

(d) Name three measures taken to help farmers obtain credit, protect their income or sell their produce. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) It employs a very large share of the workforce and feeds the population; it supplies raw materials to agro-based industries and earns foreign exchange through exports.

(b) The division of a farmer’s land into many small, scattered plots, mostly through inheritance. Effect: time and labour are wasted and machines or wells cannot be used efficiently.

(c) Monsoon rain is uncertain in timing and amount and unevenly spread, so droughts or floods destroy rain-fed crops. Remedies: expand irrigation such as canals, tube wells, farm ponds and drip; grow drought-resistant varieties; manage watersheds.

(d) Kisan Credit Card and cooperative or rural banks for cheap credit; crop insurance against crop failure; minimum support prices and regulated markets for fair prices (also cold storage).

questions.solution_md: Importance; fragmentation; monsoon; measures.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is meant by the Green Revolution? [2]

(b) Name the two crops and two states that gained most from it. [2]

(c) State three positive effects of the first Green Revolution. [3]

(d) State three negative effects of the first Green Revolution. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The rapid increase in food-grain production in India from the mid-1960s, achieved through high-yielding variety seeds, assured irrigation, chemical fertilisers and pesticides, machines and credit.

(b) Crops: wheat and rice. States: Punjab and Haryana (also western Uttar Pradesh).

(c) Self-sufficiency in food grains; buffer stocks against famine; higher farm incomes and growth of industries making fertilisers, pumps and tractors.

(d) Regional inequality between irrigated and rain-fed areas; neglect of pulses and millets; falling water tables, waterlogging, salinity and chemical pollution (also small farmers gained less).

questions.solution_md: Meaning; crops and states; positive; negative.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Distinguish between subsistence and commercial farming. [2]

(b) Give two differences between intensive and extensive farming. [2]

(c) State three features of plantation farming and name two plantation crops of India with a state for each. [3]

(d) What is mixed farming? Give two advantages of it. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Subsistence farming grows crops mainly for the farmer’s family, on small plots with simple tools; commercial farming grows crops mainly for sale, using bought inputs such as HYV seeds, fertilisers and machines.

(b) Intensive: small farms, much labour per hectare, high yield per hectare, multiple cropping. Extensive: large farms, machines, low yield per hectare but high output per worker, usually one crop.

(c) A single cash crop on a large estate; large capital and many hired workers; processing on or near the estate and production mainly for sale or export. Examples: tea — Assam; coffee — Karnataka (rubber — Kerala).

(d) Growing crops and rearing livestock together on the same farm. Advantages: milk and animal products give a steady income; dung manures the fields while crops provide fodder, so costs fall and risk is spread.

questions.solution_md: Subsistence/commercial; intensive/extensive; plantation; mixed.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Name the months of sowing and harvesting of kharif crops and two kharif crops. [2]

(b) Why is light winter rain in Punjab and Haryana useful for rabi crops? Name its source. [2]

(c) What is the zayad season? Why are zayad crops usually grown on irrigated land? [3]

(d) An illustrative farm has a net sown area of 4 ha and grows crops on 4 ha in kharif, 3 ha in rabi and 1 ha in zayad. Calculate its cropping intensity and state what the value shows. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Sown in June–July with the onset of the south-west monsoon, harvested in September–October; rice and cotton (also jowar, bajra, maize, groundnut, jute).

(b) The rabi crops such as wheat grow in the dry winter; light showers add moisture to the soil during growth and reduce the need for irrigation. The rain comes from western disturbances.

(c) A short season from about March to June between the rabi harvest and kharif sowing, for quick crops such as watermelon, cucumber and vegetables. The months are hot and dry with little rain, so the crops need irrigation.

(d) Gross cropped area $= 4 + 3 + 1 = 8$ ha; intensity $= \dfrac{8}{4} \times 100 = 200$%. Each hectare carries two crops a year on average — intensive use of land made possible by irrigation.

questions.solution_md: Kharif; western disturbances; zayad; 200%.

questions.stem_md:
Study the illustrative wheat yields of District P (tonnes per hectare): 1960: 1.0; 1970: 2.0; 1980: 2.8; 1990: 3.5; 2000: 4.2. In 2000 the district had 250 thousand hectares under wheat.

(a) Calculate the percentage rise in yield between 1960 and 1980. [2]

(b) Calculate the district’s wheat production in 2000. [2]

(c) Give three reasons for the rise in yield after 1960. [3]

(d) State two problems that such rapid growth may have caused in the district, and suggest one remedy. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\dfrac{2.8 - 1.0}{1.0} \times 100 = 180$%.

(b) Production $= 4.2 \times 250 = 1050$ thousand tonnes.

(c) Sowing of HYV wheat seeds; assured irrigation from canals and tube wells; greater use of fertilisers and pesticides, supported by credit and minimum support prices.

(d) Falling water table from heavy pumping; soil salinity or loss of fertility from overuse of water and chemicals (also neglect of pulses, inequality). Remedy: drip irrigation and crop diversification, or soil testing and organic manure.

questions.solution_md: 180%; 1050 thousand tonnes; reasons; problems and remedy.
